content: We noticed recently that Nat.Coprime.card_divisors_mul lives in Mathlib.NumberTheory.ArithmeticFunction.Misc, even though the statement has nothing to do with ArithmeticFunctions (the one line proof does use ArithmeticFunctions). Is this the "right" decision? (Same with Nat.Coprime.sum_divisors_mul) There's obviously a (presumably longer) proof that doesn't pass through the data in ArithmeticFunctions, so must one import ArithmeticFunctions to get access to the fact that divisors multiply? Git blame says to ask @David Loeffler, but this is a more general question; I'm trying to learn something about proper library design: if you have a statement that in principle is only about a simple object X and can be proved either: directly but with a longer argument, or using a big machine Y that anyone wanting to use X would henceforth have to import, do you go for the former or latter? Maybe the answer is "it depends"? (This is not a big deal, obviously, I'm just curious about Mathlib decision-making in this setting...)

PS This also affects theorem searching: if you expect something about divisors to be near other theorems about divisors, but it's actually all the way over in ArithmeticFunctions, you wouldn't find it as easily...

PPS Maybe this means that some of the theorems used in the construction of this proof involving ArithmeticFunctions belong in Nat.Coprime or something, and card_divisors_mul should live there, and then the ArithmeticFunctions technology should call on those theorems? I was just surprised to find the theorem where it was... Thanks for your advice!
I think that in general it depends on how big is the import and on how bigger is the other proof. Another possibility is to create a new file.
Pretty sure I didn’t write that code, only split up a pre-existing larger file into pieces. I agree it is ok to put up with slightly longer proofs in order to keep related statements together.

FWIW these are from #14597 by Lawrence Wu (llllvvuu)
I think ArithmeticFunction isn't a "big machine", so in this case it's fine, but it reminds me of these similar situations:

  • Should docs#Nat.fib be defined as a docs#LinearRecurrence ?
  • Should docs#Nat.totient be defined as an docs#ArithmeticFunction ?

I remember a discussion a few months ago where everyone was in favor of making Nat.totient an ArithmeticFunction (but I forgot where it was), and I believe that's what mathematicians would expect (I think the concept of a multiplicative function was motivated by the totient function?)

• Should docs#Nat.fib be defined as a docs#LinearRecurrence ?

A LinearRecurrence doesn't actually contain the data for the function ℕ → R. Maybe it should? And then you can prove an extensionality principle that actually, the other two fields completely characterize the linear recurrence.
surely you also need the initial conditions?
otherwise you also get e.g. the Lucas numbers
Oh yeah. I guess LinearRecurrence is really the "shape" of a linear recurrence, rather than any particular one.
So then the answer to your question is "no, that wouldn't even make sense"
By the way, we PRed the proposed move, please see #36495. This got hit with a large import label; not sure if that means we should branch off into a separate file?
